hints: Notice in the diagram that $R_1$ and $R_2$ share the same middle wire with no junction, while $R_3$ forms a separate lower branch between the same two dots.
Recall that resistors on the same single path add directly, while resistors on separate branches between the same two nodes add by reciprocals.
First combine $R_1$ and $R_2$ into one series value, then combine that value with $R_3$ using the parallel rule for $R_T$.
walkthrough: Identify the connections from the dots in the diagram: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are end-to-end on the upper branch, so the same current must pass through both.
For two resistors in series, the combined resistance is the sum, so the upper branch has resistance $R_{12} = R_1 + R_2$.
The upper branch $R_{12}$ and the lower resistor $R_3$ both connect between the same left and right nodes, so they are in parallel and share the same potential difference.
For two resistors in parallel, reciprocals add: $1/R_T = 1/R_{12} + 1/R_3$.
Substitute $R_{12} = R_1 + R_2$ to get $1/R_T = 1/(R_1+R_2) + 1/R_3$. This is option D.

options.A: This adds all three as $R_1 + R_2 + R_3$, which would only be correct if all three were in series with the same current.
options.B: The right-hand side $1/(R_1+R_2) + 1/R_3$ has unit $\Omega^{-1}$, so it cannot equal $R_T$ which has unit $\Omega$.
options.C: This treats $R_1 + R_2 + R_3$ as a single series branch in parallel, but $R_3$ is a separate parallel branch from $R_1$ and $R_2$.
options.D: The series pair gives $R_1 + R_2$ in parallel with $R_3$, so $1/R_T = 1/(R_1+R_2) + 1/R_3$.
